author: A Robot
objectives: Students will identify and name the four chambers of the heart, the four heart valves, and the major vessels entering and leaving the heart.
Students will trace the path of blood through the heart's dual circulation, naming each chamber, valve, and vessel in order.
Students will distinguish the pulmonary circuit from the systemic circuit and explain why the right and left sides of the heart serve different circulatory functions.

Students will explain why the left ventricle has a substantially thicker myocardium than the right ventricle, relating wall thickness to the pressure required to perfuse the systemic versus pulmonary circuits.
Students will describe the function of the atrioventricular and semilunar valves in preventing backflow, and identify which valves separate which chambers or chamber-vessel pairs.

modules.description: An overview of the heart's exterior and interior gross structure and its anatomical orientation.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the basic external and internal orientation of the human heart.
Explain why anatomical left and right are reversed from the viewer's perspective.
instructions: Look at the two heart models on the table.
Rotate them using your controller to observe external vs internal structures.
Observe the anatomical left and right labels.

clips.changeMeaning: Show side-by-side models of intact and cutaway heart for initial gross anatomical observation.
clips.narration: Welcome to the Cardiovascular Anatomy lab. Before you are two highly accurate human heart models. On your left is an intact heart showing the external features and great vessels. On your right is a cutaway model exposing the inner chambers, valves, and septum. Take a moment to examine their shapes and orientations.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight anatomical direction labels to explain left/right orientation reversal.
clips.narration: Notice the labels 'Anatomical Left' and 'Anatomical Right'. In anatomy, we always describe orientation from the perspective of the patient's own body, not the viewer. Therefore, the left side of the heart is on your physical right, and the right side is on your physical left. Keep this rule in mind throughout our tour!

modules.description: A detailed guided structural tour highlighting the chambers, valves, and major vessels.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify and name the four chambers of the heart.
Identify and locate the four heart valves.
Map interior structures to corresponding exterior vascular landmarks.
instructions: Observe the pointer highlighting structures in sequence.
Locate each chamber, valve, and major vessel on the heart models.

components.text: Heart Chambers: Right Atrium, Right Ventricle, Left Atrium, Left Ventricle

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight heart chambers sequentially by moving the indicator pointer.
clips.narration: Let's tour the inner anatomy. The heart has four chambers. The top chambers are the right and left atria, which receive returning blood. The bottom chambers are the thick-walled right and left ventricles, which pump blood out of the heart. Locate them on your cutaway model now.

clips.changeMeaning: Move pointer to the location of the heart valves and update instructions.
clips.narration: Four valves keep blood flowing in one direction. The right side has the Tricuspid Valve between the atrium and ventricle, and the Pulmonary Valve leading to the lungs. The left side features the Mitral or Bicuspid Valve, and the Aortic Valve leading to the main body. The dual-naming 'mitral' and 'bicuspid' is common in clinical vs academic settings.

components.text: Great Vessels: Vena Cavae, Pulmonary Trunk/Veins, Aorta

clips.changeMeaning: Move indicator pointer to highlight key blood vessels.
clips.narration: Finally, observe the great vessels. Deoxygenated blood returns via the Superior and Inferior Vena Cava. The Pulmonary Trunk and Arteries carry it to the lungs. Oxygenated blood returns via the Pulmonary Veins and exits the heart into systemic circulation through the massive Aorta.

modules.description: Introduces the continuous flow and color coding of systemic and pulmonary circulation.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Distinguish between the pulmonary circuit and systemic circuit.
State the oxygenation status of blood in different sides of the heart.
instructions: Observe the moving red and blue streams in the heart model.
Understand the functional split between left (oxygenated) and right (deoxygenated) chambers.

clips.changeMeaning: Show color-coded blood streams inside the cutaway heart representing oxygenation states.
clips.narration: The heart drives two distinct loops, or circuits, of blood flow. By convention, blue represents deoxygenated blood, rich in carbon dioxide, while red represents oxygenated blood, fresh from the lungs. Let's look at how the heart keeps these separate.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight the pulmonary circuit by scaling it up and changing the central label text.
clips.narration: The Pulmonary Circuit is powered by the right side of the heart. Deoxygenated blood returns from the body, is collected in the right atrium and ventricle, and is pumped out to the lungs to exchange carbon dioxide for oxygen. This is a shorter, lower-pressure circuit.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight the systemic circuit by scaling it up and scaling down the pulmonary loop.
clips.narration: The Systemic Circuit is driven by the left side of the heart. Highly oxygenated blood returning from the lungs enters the left atrium and ventricle, and is forcefully ejected into the aorta to nourish cells across the entire body before returning to start the cycle again.

modules.description: Trace a single red blood cell step-by-step through the dual circulatory system.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace the precise path of blood through the heart's chambers, valves, and vessels.
Identify where blood switches from deoxygenated to oxygenated.
instructions: Use the Next button to step the red blood cell along the flow path.
Observe the color and position changes of the cell.

clips.changeMeaning: Position the red blood cell in the Superior Vena Cava and show initial label.
clips.narration: Let's follow a single red blood cell. We start in the Superior Vena Cava, returning deoxygenated from the upper tissues of the body. Press next to trace its pathway.

components.text: Step 2: Right Atrium -> Tricuspid Valve -> Right Ventricle

clips.changeMeaning: Move cell into the right atrium and then ventricle via the tricuspid valve.
clips.narration: The cell enters the right atrium. As the atrium contracts, the cell passes through the tricuspid valve and is pushed down into the right ventricle, which will pump it to the lungs.

clips.changeMeaning: Move cell out the pulmonary valve to pulmonary trunk and transition color to red representing oxygenation.
clips.narration: Ventricular contraction drives the cell through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary arteries. In the lung capillaries, the cell releases carbon dioxide and binds fresh oxygen, turning bright red.

components.text: Step 4: Pulmonary Veins -> Left Atrium -> Mitral -> Left Ventricle

clips.changeMeaning: Move cell from pulmonary veins into the left atrium and down through the mitral valve to the left ventricle.
clips.narration: The oxygenated cell returns via pulmonary veins to the left atrium. It passes through the mitral valve into the thick-walled left ventricle, preparing for systemic propulsion.

components.text: Step 5: Aortic Valve -> Aorta -> Body Systemic Circulation

clips.changeMeaning: Move cell through the aortic valve into the aorta to systemic tissues.
clips.narration: The left ventricle contracts with massive pressure, launching the cell through the aortic valve into the aorta. It is now on its way to supply oxygen to the body's tissues before returning blue.

modules.description: Analyze the anatomical differences between ventricular wall thickness and their physiologic cause.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain why the left ventricle wall is substantially thicker than the right.
Relate myocardial wall thickness to vascular circuit pressure requirements.
instructions: Compare the right and left ventricle wall thicknesses.
Review the scale markers detailing the 3-to-1 thickness ratio.

clips.changeMeaning: Display horizontal cross sections of right and left ventricle to evaluate thickness difference.
clips.narration: Why are the ventricle walls shaped so differently? Look closely at this horizontal cross-section through the ventricles. Notice that the right ventricle wall on your left is thin, whereas the left ventricle wall on your right is robust and muscular.

components.text: Left Ventricle is ~3x thicker than Right Ventricle due to high systemic resistance.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight numerical thickness scale markers and explain the physiological pressure differential.
clips.narration: The healthy right ventricle wall measures 3 to 5 millimeters, pumping to the lungs' low-resistance capillaries. The left ventricle wall is 10 to 15 millimeters thick—about a three-to-one ratio! It needs massive pressure to pump blood through the high-resistance blood vessels of the entire systemic body loop.

modules.description: Demonstrates structural states of AV and Semilunar valves during systole and diastole.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Describe the function of atrioventricular and semilunar valves in preventing backflow.
Contrast valve opening states during contraction (systole) versus relaxation (diastole).
instructions: Compare the mechanical state of AV and Semilunar valves during the cardiac cycle.
Step between Systole and Diastole modes to see the reciprocal operation.

components.scriptDescription: Manages alternating 3D models of cardiac valves, toggling active states of open vs closed meshes for AV and Semilunar valves in response to cyclical phases.

components.text: Ventricular Systole: AV Valves Closed, Semilunar Valves Open

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight AV valves and demonstrate contraction/systole state.
clips.narration: Heart valves operate dynamically to prevent blood backflow. Atrioventricular (AV) valves sit between the chambers, while semilunar valves control blood entering the arteries. During ventricular contraction, or Systole, high pressure snaps AV valves shut to prevent blood leaking back into the atria, while semilunar valves are forced wide open.

components.text: Ventricular Diastole: AV Valves Open, Semilunar Valves Closed

clips.changeMeaning: Show relaxation/diastole state of the valves.
clips.narration: When the ventricles relax, or Diastole, the pressure drops. AV valves hang open so atria can fill the ventricles. Simultaneously, the semilunar valves snap shut to prevent blood in the great arteries from draining backward into the relaxed ventricles.

Demonstrate recall of cardiac structure names.

Differentiate the sequential roles of chambers, valves, and vessel pathways.

components.text:
Blood Flow Sequencing Quiz
Blood has just entered the Right Atrium. Where does it go next?

clips.changeMeaning: Start the sequencing flow quiz to practice pathway logic.
clips.narration: Now, let's test your ability to trace blood flow. In this quiz, you will be given a starting location, such as the Right Atrium, and you must select the next structure in the correct physiological flow sequence. Good luck!

modules.description: A summary recapping the anatomical and physiologic principles explored in the lab.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Consolidate overall cardiac structures, functions, and circulatory pathways.
instructions: Review the summary points shown on the display.

components.text:
Lab Recap:
1. Four Chambers & Great Vessels
2. Dual Circuits (Pulmonary & Systemic)
3. 3-to-1 Ventricular Myocardium Ratio
4. One-way Valve Backflow Prevention

clips.changeMeaning: Display summary board and run through key learning outcomes.
clips.narration: Excellent work completing this lab! We've covered the internal and external gross anatomy, mapped the separate pulmonary and systemic circuits, traced a red blood cell's oxygenation loop, compared ventricular wall thicknesses, and observed dynamic valve backflow prevention. Thank you for participating.
